solve.my_answer: Kernel: the fixed T-dependent shape kappa(T;s,l,g) = [g<T]*r, with r = min(l, max(0, T-s)) for l>0 and r = 1 for l=0. Here s is the start, l the length and g the gate. Its special cases are constant, atom, year cell, gated year cell and density. Amplitude a_j: the T-independent multiplier of a kernel, computed by masked sum-of-products (Ch.3). Node: a point where the value or slope changes, i.e. an event time or a year boundary. Jump form (c0,c1): each kernel split into pieces [u<T](c0 + c1*T) placed at nodes u; the jump at u is c0 + c1*u and the slope change is c1. Relation: Phi(T) = sum_j a_j*kappa_j(T); splitting every kernel into node pieces and summing (c0,c1) per node gives Phi(T) = initial value + sum over u<T of (c0(u) + c1(u)*T).

solve.my_answer: (a) Yes. y_t = rho x_t is a convolution with response h_0 = rho and h_k = 0 for k >= 1. It is linear and time-invariant (proportional relation). (b) No. This is a gate: the renewal time tau switches off the repair rate and cancels that year's portion. A 0/1 factor fixed by the event time multiplies the repair, so the relation is nonlinear in the event time and is not a fixed response shape that superposes. (c) No. This is a state (memory) relation. The response h(t,s) = r GWP m0 q^(t-s) [no replacement between s and t] depends on whether a replacement happened in between, not only on t - s, so it is not time-invariant. A later replacement cuts the effect of an earlier fill, so effects do not add over the replacement sequence. It must be written as the recurrence (6.2).

solve.my_answer: (1) Every function computed by a finite combination of the 2 structures is piecewise rational. Masked sums of products use column values, 0/1 comparisons and the 1-column functions 1/a, 1-a, 1/(1-a), a/(1-a). Node spectra are piecewise linear in T. So the input space splits into finitely many pieces, and on each piece the function is a ratio of polynomials. x^0.5 and log10 x are not rational on any interval, however small, so no such function can equal them on an interval as a real function. (2) The goal is different. For each double-precision input (a finite set), return the double nearest the true value. With finitely many inputs, a finite partition into pieces (masks or thresholds), or in principle a finite table, achieves this. This does not contradict (1): (1) is about equality of real functions on intervals, which is impossible; (2) is about identical outputs at finite precision, which is possible. (3) The bound is about failure probability under the declared distribution. The band has relative width of about 1e-9, so the distribution gives it almost zero probability and samples practically never land there (and only integer T were checked, 9.8). Failures concentrated there would not change the bound. The research therefore restricted its claim to D', which excludes the band.

It never says why. The key idea is missing: there are finitely many double inputs, so any map from doubles to doubles (for example the correctly rounded result) can be built with a finite partition or table using masks, or with a rational approximation plus threshold corrections. That is still piecewise rational with finitely many pieces. Without it a beginner can only repeat the claim. It should be added to 9.5, ideally with a small example. Section 9.5 also asserts without even a sketch that x^a and log10 x are not rational on any interval.
solve.official_answer_error: The official (2) relies on the argument that 'there are finitely many double inputs, so a finite table or partition can be built', but problems.json marks external: null. solve.problem_defect: Part (2) asks why the research 'can say' the function is realized exactly at double precision, but the textbook gives no mechanism. A student can only restate 9.5 or bring in outside reasoning, so it is not answerable from the textbook alone.
solve.external_knowledge: Doubles form a finite set, so any function on them can be realized by a finite table or piecewise construction (for example, correct rounding by enumeration or by a rational approximation with an error below half an ulp, corrected by comparisons).
